eyebrow: Local's Guide to Chai Nat · Updated 2026
intro: Chai Nat is a small town on the Chao Phraya River packed with more good things than most people expect — from Asia's largest open-flight aviary and Thailand's first river barrage dam to Luang Pu Suk's famous temple and the ancient chedis of the old town of Phraek Si Racha. We've gathered the 10 attractions visitors to Chai Nat talk about most, all in one place — a single day's drive covers several spots without any rush.
chips: 🦜 Chai Nat Bird Park, Asia's largest open aviary
🌅 Chao Phraya Dam, Thailand's first dam
🛕 Luang Pu Suk's temple at Pak Khlong Makham Thao
🏛️ Ancient chedis of Sankhaburi old town

blocks.html:
Chai Nat is a small province in the Chao Phraya River basin, about two and a half hours north of Bangkok. Its charm is the sheer variety packed close together — nature, temple visits, and easygoing riverside time all fit in one trip. Start the morning at Chai Nat Bird Park at the foot of Khao Tha Phra, wandering a giant open aviary; head north late morning to pay respects to Luang Pho Thammachak at Wat Thammamun on the Chao Phraya; stop by Luang Pu Suk's Wat Pak Khlong Makham Thao in Wat Sing district in the afternoon; then finish at Chao Phraya Dam, catching a cool breeze as the sun sets. And if your visit lands on the first weekend of the month, add a stroll through the retro-style Sapphaya Old Police Station Market. A Chai Nat trip works equally well for families, photographers, and anyone who wants to escape the city and unwind.

Many places on this list are icons of the province. The true headliner is Chai Nat Bird Park, whose 26-rai open aviary is billed as the largest in Asia, gathering more than 100 bird species in one place, plus a water park, a bird-egg museum, and an aquarium showcasing fish of the Chao Phraya basin. Wat Pak Khlong Makham Thao is the temple of Luang Pu Suk Kesaro, the famed master monk; inside its ordination hall are murals painted by Prince Chumphon of Songkhla — Krom Luang Chumphon Khet Udomsak, affectionately called "Sadet Tia" — Luang Pu Suk's foremost disciple, still there for visitors to admire today. Chao Phraya Dam was the country's first river barrage, with a long walkway for catching the breeze and cycling along the crest. And Sankhaburi old town offers a square chedi in U Thong–Lopburi style and a star-fruit-ribbed prang to delight lovers of ancient monuments. Tick them all off and you'll understand why this little town on the Chao Phraya keeps drawing people back.

blocks.name: Chai Nat Bird Park
blocks.area: Khao Tha Phra subdistrict, Mueang Chai Nat district
blocks.signature: A 26-rai open aviary, the largest in Asia, home to over 100 bird species, plus the Space Water Park, a bird-egg museum, and the Chao Phraya Basin fish aquarium
blocks.descHtml:
Ask anyone to name the first attraction that comes to mind in Chai Nat and the answer is "Chai Nat Bird Park." Open since 1983, it has long since become the province's landmark. The star here is the 26-rai open aviary, claimed to be the largest in Asia — netting stretched over the entire grounds, with more than 100 bird species living together in near-natural conditions. You walk right into the aviary itself and meet peacocks, cranes, hawks, and eagles flying overhead. It's ideal for families who want their kids to see real birds up close, not peering through little cage bars.

Beyond the giant aviary, the full 248-rai grounds hold plenty more to keep children entertained all day. A favorite in many reviews is the Chao Phraya Basin fish aquarium, with over 90 freshwater species and a walk-through fish tunnel kids adore. The bird-egg museum is a quirky stop too, gathering eggs of many species, and there's a planetarium plus a straw eagle sculpture said to be the only one of its kind in Thailand. The hot-season highlight is the "Space Water Park," with slides for kids to cool off (it charges a separate entry fee, but an affordable one).

Admission is a real bargain for everything you get to see: Thai adults ฿60, children ฿25; foreign adults ฿150, children ฿75. Seniors, visitors with disabilities, and Chai Nat residents enter free. Open daily 08:30–17:00. The grounds are shady and green overall, though some reviews say frankly that certain areas look worn and could use more upkeep, and some ponds run dry in the dry season — worth keeping expectations in check.

The location is an easy drive, right on Phahonyothin Road (Highway 1) at the foot of Khao Phlong in Khao Tha Phra subdistrict, about 4 kilometers before Chai Nat town — convenient for anyone passing through. It's popular because it bundles so much into one place — birdwatching, fish, a water park, room for kids to run — for mere tens of baht. Set aside half a day, wear comfortable walking shoes, and bring a hat and water, because the grounds are bigger and involve more walking than you'd think. A fitting first stop of a family-friendly Chai Nat trip.
mustOrder: Walk the 26-rai open aviary, the largest in Asia
The fish tunnel / Chao Phraya Basin aquarium
Space Water Park (a cool-off in hot season)
Bird-egg museum + the straw eagle sculpture
blocks.bestFor: Whole-family outings with kids, easily a full day of walking

Photo by Mr.Peerapong Prasutr / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

blocks.name: Chao Phraya Dam
blocks.signature: Thailand's first river barrage dam — a long walkway for riverside breezes, a sunset viewpoint, and early-morning cycling along the dam crest
blocks.descHtml:
If you're passing through Chai Nat and want somewhere to relax without spending a baht, Chao Phraya Dam in Bang Luang subdistrict, Sapphaya district, is the spot locals keep recommending to each other. Its claim to fame is being Thailand's first large river barrage, completed back in 1957. The reinforced-concrete structure stretches more than 237 meters, with 16 sluice gates spanning the Chao Phraya River and a long footbridge crossing to the far bank. It suits anyone who enjoys quiet riverside scenery, families out for a stroll, and cyclists after wide-open views.

The highlight visitors mention most is the evening: walking the bridge over the dam crest in a cool breeze, watching the sun slowly sink behind the river. Real reviewers say mid-afternoon is a touch too sunny — come around 5 pm when the light softens and the walk gets far more comfortable. Another popular angle is standing to watch the water rush through the sluice gates; in flood season the current runs impressively fierce. Early risers will regularly meet groups of cyclists riding up for the views along the crest, in cool air under lovely skies.

No need to worry about budget — entry is free, with a large free parking area and decently clean restrooms. Around the dam there's a royal commemorative park for strolling, plus a fish market and riverside restaurants to visit afterward. It isn't far from Chai Nat town: take the turnoff toward Sapphaya district for about 6 kilometers and you're there. It's open all day, but the best windows are early morning and evening.

A few things to know: cars aren't allowed up on the dam crest — park below and walk up. The place stays simple and natural rather than a polished tourist attraction; its charm lies in the calm and the wide river views. If you expect lots of activities you may find it quiet, but if you've come to rest your eyes, catch the breeze, and photograph the sunset, it delivers with ease — a great stop along a 2-day-1-night Chai Nat trip.
mustOrder: Walk the bridge over the dam crest for Chao Phraya river breezes
Watch the sunset around 5 pm as the light softens
Cycle along the dam crest at dawn
See the current surge through the sluice gates (especially in flood season)
blocks.bestFor: Evening breeze-and-sunset strolls, or early-morning cycling on the dam crest
blocks.hours: Open daily 24 hours (crest best at dawn and dusk)
blocks.libCredit: Photo by Mr. Peerapong Prasutr / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

blocks.name: Wat Thammamun Worawihan
blocks.signature: A royal temple on the slopes of Khao Thammamun beside the Chao Phraya — a 565-step hillside stairway, home to Luang Pho Thammachak, a standing Buddha in the calming-relatives pose on a lotus base, blending Chiang Saen–Sukhothai and Ayutthaya art
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Thammamun Worawihan is Chai Nat's revered royal temple, set on the slopes of Khao Thammamun beside the Chao Phraya River. It's an old temple believed to date back to the Sukhothai era and restored through the Ayutthaya period. It's a great fit for blessing-seekers, lovers of temple history and art, and families making a merit stop along the old Chai Nat–Nakhon Sawan road. The highlight is Luang Pho Thammachak, a standing Buddha in the calming-relatives pose on a lotus base, beautiful in a blend of Chiang Saen–early Sukhothai and Ayutthaya styles, with a dharma wheel mark on the palm that gives the image its name.

Don't miss the 565-step stairway up the hill behind the temple, leading to the shrine of Luang Pho Nak on the summit. At the top you get a sweeping view of the Chao Phraya's bend and Chai Nat town spread wide below. Many visitors say it's breezy, cool, and wonderfully quiet up there. If the full climb is too much, you can pay respects to Luang Pho Thammachak and make offerings down below instead. The grounds are shady with big trees and plenty of parking.

Another charm is the riverside market along the bank under the bridge in front of the temple, where villagers sell homestyle snacks and farm produce at friendly prices. Many reviewers love sitting with their legs dangling over the Chao Phraya, eating a bowl of noodles after their temple visit — merit made and stomach filled in one go.

Entry is free, with no admission fee, open roughly 08:00–18:00 daily. Its Google rating sits around 4.7 from reviews numbering in the thousands, reflecting how warmly both Chai Nat locals and travelers speak of it. Worth knowing: if you plan to climb the 565 steps, wear comfortable shoes and carry water — the midday sun is fairly strong. Come in the morning or evening for an easier walk and prettier view photos.
mustOrder: Pay respects to Luang Pho Thammachak, the calming-relatives Buddha on a lotus base
Climb the 565 steps to Luang Pho Nak's shrine on the summit
Take in the view of the Chao Phraya's bend from the hilltop
Dangling-legs noodles at the riverside market in front of the temple
blocks.bestFor: Temple blessings, river views, and a stop at the riverside market
blocks.libCredit: Photo by KOSIN SUKHUM / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

blocks.name: Wat Pak Khlong Makham Thao
blocks.signature: The temple of Luang Pu Suk Kesaro, the famed master monk — inside the ordination hall are murals painted by Krom Luang Chumphon Khet Udomsak (Sadet Tia), his foremost disciple
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Pak Khlong Makham Thao — known to everyone simply as "Luang Pu Suk's temple" — is an old temple on the Tha Chin River at the mouth of Makham Thao canal in Wat Sing district, Chai Nat, and a near-obligatory stop for anyone passing through the province. Its significance: Phra Khru Wimon Khunakon (Luang Pu Suk Kesaro), the renowned master monk of the amulet tradition, once served as abbot here, and he was also the teacher of Krom Luang Chumphon Khet Udomsak (Sadet Tia), the foremost disciple revered across the country. If you love blessings, prayers, or temples with real stories and history, this one fits the bill perfectly.

The can't-miss highlight is the ordination hall, whose interior murals were painted "by the hand of Prince Chumphon" himself, offered to Luang Pu Suk when the hall was built — a rarity you won't see anywhere else. Afterward, pay respects at the cast statues of Luang Pu Suk and Prince Chumphon, walk beneath the statue base for good fortune, and wander past the old mondop, Luang Pu Suk's original monastic quarters, and the Guanyin shrine by the river. Many come to pray for protection from harm, safety, and success in trade.

The atmosphere is shady, peaceful, and far less crowded than famous big-city temples. Its setting on the Tha Chin River keeps a cool breeze going as you make your rounds. Real reviews often note that the temple is clean, the people there kind, and that morning or late-afternoon visits beat the harsh midday sun. Entry is free — it's a temple open to the public — with only voluntary donations and an amulet counter if you're interested.

As for location, the temple sits about 25 km from Chai Nat town along Highway 3183 around the km 36–37 marker. It's an easy drive with parking, open daily roughly 08:00–17:00 (the ordination hall may close over midday, so allow extra time). Dress modestly for the temple, and if you want to see the full set of murals, time your visit for when the hall is open. It's popular because it gathers sanctity, history, and rare art all in one place.
mustOrder: Pay respects at the cast statue of Luang Pu Suk Kesaro
See Prince Chumphon's hand-painted murals in the ordination hall
Honor the statue of Krom Luang Chumphon (Sadet Tia)
Visit the Guanyin shrine on the Tha Chin River
blocks.bestFor: Blessing-seekers honoring a famed master monk — best in morning or afternoon
blocks.libCredit: Photo by Mr. Peerapong Prasutr / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

blocks.name: Sapphaya Old Police Station Market (Green Dee Market)
blocks.signature: A retro community market at an old police station — vendors in period dress, local eats, a foam-free and single-use-plastic-free concept; open the first Saturday–Sunday of each month, 15:00–20:00
blocks.descHtml:
The Sapphaya Old Police Station Market — known to many as "Green Dee Market" — is a retro community market on the Chao Phraya River in Sapphaya district. Its centerpiece is the old wooden police station dating to R.S. 120 (around 1901), counted among the oldest police stations in Thailand, which earned an architectural conservation award from the Association of Siamese Architects in 2018 and now houses a small museum of old photographs and community stories. It's a great fit for easygoing wanderers who love a bygone-days atmosphere and want a break from the usual markets for one with genuine historical character.

The must-see highlight is the riverside walking street lined with old wooden houses stretching some 300 meters. Many vendors dress in traditional Thai period costume, selling local dishes and hard-to-find old-fashioned Thai sweets, with playfully clever menu items like the "jail-cell oliang" iced coffee that riffs on the old-police-station theme. Keep strolling and you'll find street-art corners for photos. Most reviews love that the market still genuinely belongs to the villagers — it isn't a staged set, prices are friendly with snacks starting at just tens of baht, and it's Chai Nat's first foam-free, single-use-plastic-free market, using banana leaves and bamboo tubes instead.

Budget-wise it's very easy: entry is free, and you pay only for food and souvenirs. It sits on the Chao Phraya in Sapphaya subdistrict, a short drive from Chai Nat town. The key detail to remember is that the "Green Dee" market opens only on the first Saturday–Sunday of each month, 15:00–21:00 (the old police station and the community can be visited during the day on weekdays, but the stalls are liveliest on market days). Its fame keeps growing — it won a Thailand Tourism Gold Awards for community-based tourism and gets cited as a model eco-friendly market among Thailand's secondary cities.

Worth knowing: if you're set on the full evening market experience, double-check that your dates fall on the first weekend of the month, or you'll find only a quiet community. Late afternoon brings soft light and a pleasant river breeze. Bringing a cloth bag or a tiffin carrier fits the plastic-free theme perfectly, and carry cash, since most vendors are local villagers who deal mainly in cash.
mustOrder: "Jail-cell oliang," the market's signature drink
Old-fashioned Thai sweets fresh from community vendors' stoves
Photos in front of the R.S. 120 (1901) wooden police station + riverside street art
Stroll past the old wooden houses along the Chao Phraya
blocks.bestFor: Retro-market strolls and local eats — come the first Saturday–Sunday of the month

blocks.title: 🛏️ Where to Stay in Chai Nat
blocks.text: If you'd rather explore Chai Nat without rushing the drive back, spend a night in town or along the Chao Phraya. There are small hotels, riverside resorts, and friendly-priced guesthouses in good locations near the bird park and the main sights — wake up early to visit temples or head back to the bird park with ease. Booking ahead through an app gets you better rates and first pick of the rooms with a view.

blocks.name: Chai Nat Muni National Museum
blocks.area: Chai Nat subdistrict, Mueang Chai Nat district
blocks.signature: A two-story applied-Thai-style museum displaying artifacts from prehistory through the Dvaravati era, plus Buddha images and ceramics in Lopburi, Sukhothai, Ayutthaya, and Rattanakosin styles
blocks.descHtml:
If you're the type who enjoys browsing antiquities quietly and without hurry, the Chai Nat Muni National Museum is a stop you shouldn't miss in Chai Nat. It sits within the grounds of Wat Phra Borommathat Worawihan — you can walk straight over from the temple. Its origins trace to Phra Chai Nat Muni, a former provincial ecclesiastical head who gradually collected artifacts found in Chai Nat and nearby areas, a collection now in the care of the Fine Arts Department. It suits anyone who wants a deeper understanding of the Chao Phraya basin's roots, and families bringing kids to learn some history.

The building is a two-story applied Thai design. The ground floor tells the story from prehistory — stone axes, tools, and implements — through Buddha images and ceramics of the Lopburi, Sukhothai, and Ayutthaya periods up to Rattanakosin. Upstairs, the highlights are votive-tablet molds from many eras and a bronze Buddha in the subduing-Mara pose that several sources describe as a rarely seen piece. What many reviewers appreciate is that the collection isn't so large it wears you out — each piece has a story, the information labels are easy to read, and you can finish comfortably within an hour.

Inside it's cool, quiet, and uncrowded, perfect for taking your time. Admission is ฿10 for Thais, ฿80 for foreigners; students in uniform, monks, and clergy enter free. Excellent value for what you get to see. Open Wednesday to Sunday, 09:00–16:00, closed Mondays, Tuesdays, and public holidays. Its Google rating sits around 4.3, and most visitors praise the friendly staff and their good explanations.

Worth knowing: the museum sits right beside Wat Phra Borommathat, so plan them together — pay respects at the relic stupa, then walk through the museum in the same visit. There's a fair amount of parking, and since it closes Monday–Tuesday, check the day before setting out so the trip isn't wasted.
mustOrder: The standout bronze Buddha in the subduing-Mara pose upstairs
Votive-tablet molds from many eras
Prehistoric–Dvaravati artifacts
Lopburi/Sukhothai/Ayutthaya Buddha images and ceramics
blocks.bestFor: History and antiquities fans — pair it with a visit to Wat Phra Borommathat

blocks.name: Wat Phra Kaeo, Sankhaburi
blocks.area: Sankhaburi district (Phraek Si Racha subdistrict), Chai Nat
blocks.signature: An ancient square chedi in U Thong–Lopburi style, with stucco work, a red-sandstone Buddha image, and traces of ancient Khmer artistry
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Phra Kaeo, Sankhaburi is an ancient temple in the old city zone of Phraek Si Racha, about 23 kilometers from Chai Nat town, and a superb stop for anyone who loves history and ancient architecture. The star here is a tall square chedi that many hail as the "queen of chedis in Southeast Asia." Its form is a Lavo-style chedi blended with late U Thong–Dvaravati art, its redented, tiered base strikingly unusual and beautiful. Niches on all four sides hold stucco Buddha images in the gazing pose, and the stucco work still clearly shows Sukhothai artistry mixed with early Ayutthaya, dating back some 600–700 years.

Another highlight not to miss is the shrine of Luang Pho Chai in front of the chedi, an old red-sandstone Buddha image. What reviewers often point out is the "lintel" — a stone panel carved with Khmer motifs set behind the image, placed facing upward rather than downward like typical lintels, believed to have been moved from a nearby ancient Khmer temple. Around the grounds you'll also find traces of an old ordination hall, of which only the base and red-sandstone boundary stones remain. If you enjoy poring over stone carving and stucco details, you can browse here happily.

The temple is quiet, shady, and uncrowded. Real reviews consistently say things like "an old temple, few visitors, worth preserving, with shady, charming surroundings" and "perfect for examining ancient monuments in detail" — which is why architecture photographers and temple-goers love it so much. Open daily 06:00–18:00, no entry fee, donations as you wish. Morning and evening bring soft light, the most beautiful for photographing the chedi.

Worth knowing: the temple belongs to the Sankhaburi old-town cluster, which has several ancient temples of the same era (such as Wat Mahathat, Mueang San), so you can string them into a continuous one-day trip. It sits fairly far from town, so driving yourself is most convenient. Dress modestly in the shrine area, and allow time to walk around the chedi and the old ordination-hall base — the craftsmanship holds a lot of detail.
mustOrder: The tall square chedi, the 'queen of chedis in Southeast Asia,' in U Thong–Lavo style
Luang Pho Chai, the red-sandstone Buddha + the face-up carved Khmer lintel behind it
Stucco Buddhas in the gazing pose in the chedi's four niches
Red-sandstone boundary stones around the old ordination hall
blocks.bestFor: History and architecture fans — pay respects and photograph the ancient chedi in soft morning or evening light
blocks.libCredit: Photo by KOSIN SUKHUM / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

blocks.name: Bueng Krachap Yai (Mid-Lake Island)
blocks.signature: A broad lake with a floating bamboo-raft bridge stretching across the water — a spot for waterbirds, lotus blooms, and sunsets in quiet natural surroundings
blocks.descHtml:
Bueng Krachap Yai is Chai Nat's largest freshwater lake, spanning roughly 1,116 rai, just about 2 kilometers west of Hankha town. In the middle of the lake sits an island called "Ko Mueang Thao U Thong," around 120 rai, standing prominently amid the water. The star attraction is the floating bamboo-raft bridge — a long wooden walkway resting on the water's surface that carries you across the lake to the island. It's an unseen-style nature spot that people who love quiet, rural waterside atmosphere will fall for, better suited to slow walks and deep breaths of fresh air than flashy check-in photo ops.

The thing not to miss is walking the raft bridge across to the island. Along the way the lake stretches as far as you can see, dotted with patches of lotus and plenty of waterbirds — wild ducks and Asian openbills live here in large numbers. If you like cycling, rentals run about ฿20 per bike for an easy loop around the island past everyday village life. For the best photos, come toward evening when the sun mellows, a cool breeze blows all day long, and wait for the sunset turning the water's surface gold — the moment many say is the most beautiful of the day.

Entry is free, open roughly 08:30–19:00, with the only expense being bike rental if you want to ride. Around the lake there are restaurants serving fresh fish from the lake worth stopping at. Getting there is easy since it's close to Hankha town — a regular stop for Chai Nat's cyclists and nature lovers, and it also hosts the district's annual Loy Krathong festival.

A few things to know: this is a simple natural site without many facilities, all about the quiet atmosphere. The floating raft bridge sways gently in rhythm with your steps, so small children and elderly visitors should walk with care. Morning or evening visits mean gentler sun and more waterbirds than you'd see at midday.
mustOrder: Walk the floating bamboo-raft bridge across to Ko Mueang Thao U Thong
Cycle around the island (rentals ~฿20 per bike)
Watch waterbirds, lotus blooms, and the sunset by the lake in the evening
Stop for fresh lake fish at the waterside restaurants
blocks.bestFor: Lovers of quiet nature — come for the sunset in the evening

blocks.name: Wat Phra Borommathat Worawihan
blocks.area: Chai Nat subdistrict, Mueang Chai Nat district
blocks.signature: Chai Nat's guardian stupa — a bell-shaped chedi enshrining relics of the Buddha
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Phra Borommathat Worawihan is a second-class royal temple that the people of Chai Nat revere as the province's guardian stupa. Its centerpiece is a bell-shaped chedi believed to enshrine relics of the Buddha. Culture-loving travelers, temple-goers, and anyone wanting to experience a quiet early-Ayutthaya-era temple will feel at home here, since you can pray for blessings and admire the old architecture at the same time.

The highlight many reviews agree you can't miss is the relic chedi itself, the heart of the temple. Next come the old wihan and ordination hall that preserve the original craftsmanship, along with the important Buddha images in the wihan that people come to venerate. Visit during the annual festival and you'll catch the lively cloth-wrapping ceremony around the stupa. The temple grounds also hold the Chai Nat Muni National Museum, so you can continue straight on to its artifacts and old Buddha images.

Entry is free, with donations as you wish. Open daily roughly 06:30–18:00. It's located in Chai Nat subdistrict, Mueang Chai Nat district, about 4 kilometers from town on the bank of the Chao Phraya River. Driving yourself is easiest and there's parking inside the temple; if you arrive in town by public transport, a short hired ride gets you to the temple without going far.

Worth knowing: this is an important temple with merit-makers coming through at all hours, so dress politely — skip sleeveless tops or very short shorts — and keep voices low in the wihan area. It's popular because it brings together the sanctity of the Buddha's relics, an old temple with a long history, and a museum within the same walls — one stop that covers both merit-making and history.
mustOrder: Pay homage at the bell-shaped relic chedi
Worship in the old wihan and ordination hall
Visit the Chai Nat Muni National Museum inside the temple
Come during the annual cloth-wrapping ceremony of the stupa
blocks.bestFor: Temple-goers and culture lovers — best in the cool early morning, or during the annual cloth-wrapping festival
blocks.libCredit: Photo by KOSIN SUKHUM / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

blocks.name: Wat Mahathat, Sankhaburi
blocks.area: Phraek Si Racha subdistrict, Sankhaburi district, Chai Nat
blocks.signature: Lopburi-period star-fruit-ribbed prangs, the base of an ancient great relic stupa, and old Buddha images in the ancient town of Phraek Si Racha
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Mahathat, Sankhaburi is the ancient temple of the old town of Phraek Si Racha (Mueang San), set in the heart of Sankhaburi district on the Noi River. Originally called Wat Phra That or Wat Hua Mueang, it was founded before the Ayutthaya period and restored in later eras, and the Fine Arts Department registered it as a historic monument back in 1935. It suits history-minded travelers, merit-making temple-goers, and anyone after quiet old-town photo spots without the crowds of Ayutthaya. Many who have been say the atmosphere feels like a miniature Sukhothai Historical Park — but much closer to Bangkok.

The unmissable highlight is the three "star-fruit-ribbed prangs," built of stuccoed brick on a square base in Lopburi-period style, their surfaces fluted in ridges like the lobes of an actual star fruit — a rare form and a signature of the Mueang San school of craftsmanship. Next come the large red-brick base of the great relic stupa, a cluster of chedis on octagonal bases showing U Thong artistic influence, and the ruins of the old wihan where only octagonal columns and portions of wall remain. Walking the circuit, you'll see rows of ancient Buddha images in both Lopburi and early Ayutthaya styles. The image people most come to petition is Luang Pho Lak Mueang, whom locals call Luang Pho Mo — often asked for blessings of good health.

Entry is free, with no admission fee, and a comfortable visit takes about 1–2 hours. It opens during daylight hours like temples generally do. Go in the morning or evening when the sun is soft, since the monument grounds are fairly open — the light is beautiful and the walk stays cool. The overall mood is quiet, shady, and calm, perfect for paying respects, taking photos, and soaking in the age of Mueang Phraek. It's about 20 kilometers from Chai Nat town: take Highway 340 to Sankhaburi district, then turn at the clock tower by the district office and continue about 500 meters.

It gets talked about so much because it's the masterpiece monument of Mueang San that still stands in clear view, gathering unusual prangs, ancient chedis, and old Buddha images all in one place, with consistently good Google reviews praising its beauty and tranquility. Worth knowing: it is both a sacred site and a protected monument, so dress modestly and don't climb on the ruins. And if you want the full old-town circuit, Wat Song Phi Nong, Wat Phra Kaeo, and Wat Tanot Lai are all nearby — an easy one-day trip.
mustOrder: The three star-fruit-ribbed prangs in Lopburi style
The red-brick great-stupa base + octagonal chedis in U Thong style
Pay respects to Luang Pho Lak Mueang (Luang Pho Mo)
Ancient Buddha images in Lopburi–early Ayutthaya styles

blocks.text: Chai Nat's sights are spread across several districts. Some packages include transfers from Bangkok and cover several spots in a single day — great for anyone who wants to sit back and let a local lead the way. blocks.title: Know Before You Go: Chai Nat

items.title: Renting a car or booking a tour is easiest
items.text: The sights are spread across several districts and public transport within the province is scarce. Driving yourself or hiring a car with driver from Bangkok is most convenient. Grab cars are hard to find even in Chai Nat town — don't rely on it as your main option.

items.title: Always carry cash
items.text: Temple merit-making, donation boxes, the Sapphaya Old Police Station Market, and most community food stalls take cash only. Carry small notes and coins. ATMs are available in town but hard to find at sights outside it.

items.title: Go early to beat the sun and the queues
items.text: The bird park and many riverside temples along the Chao Phraya are out in the open, and the midday sun is fierce. Mornings are more comfortable for walking and photos, and the birds are more active. Save Chao Phraya Dam for the evening sunset — the atmosphere is just right then.

items.title: Check days and hours before markets and museums
items.text: Sapphaya Old Police Station Market (Green Dee Market) opens only the first Saturday–Sunday of each month, 15:00–21:00, while the Chai Nat Muni National Museum closes Monday–Tuesday. Check each place's opening days and times before heading out so you don't miss anything.

items.title: Dress modestly for temples
items.text: Chai Nat has many temples and historic sites. Dress neatly, cover shoulders and knees when entering temple grounds or ordination halls, and remove your shoes before stepping into the wihan — etiquette the locals genuinely care about.

items.title: English is limited
items.text: Chai Nat is a secondary city visited mainly by Thai travelers, so English signs and menus are few. Carrying a translation app and saving temple names in Thai script for asking directions helps enormously. Locals are kind and happy to help.

blocks.title: How to Plan a Chai Nat Trip That Fits in One Day
blocks.html:
Chai Nat works beautifully as a day trip or short overnight from Bangkok, because the sights are spread across only a few districts — routing by zone saves the most time. Start the morning at Chai Nat Bird Park at the foot of Khao Tha Phra while the air is still cool and the birds are active; walk the open aviary and let the kids play in the water park. Then loop into town for the Chai Nat Muni National Museum and Wat Thammamun on the Chao Phraya. Late morning, cross over to the Wat Sing side to visit Luang Pu Suk's Wat Pak Khlong Makham Thao, then branch off to the ancient-monument route in Sankhaburi district — Wat Phra Kaeo and Wat Mahathat in the old town of Phraek Si Racha. Close out the evening at Chao Phraya Dam on the Sapphaya side, catching the cool breeze and the sunset from the dam crest.

Nearly all the temples and historic sites are free to enter, with donations as you wish. The stops with entry fees are Chai Nat Bird Park — Thais ฿60, foreigners ฿150, water park paid separately — and the Chai Nat Muni Museum, Thais ฿10, foreigners ฿80. The Sapphaya Old Police Station Market (Green Dee Market) opens only the first Saturday–Sunday of the month, 15:00–20:00, so slot it in only if your trip lines up with those dates. The midday sun along the Chao Phraya is quite strong — pack an umbrella, hat, and drinking water to stay comfortable — and keep the evening free for the dam, the sunset photo spot people love most

blocks.text: Seen several Chai Nat sights and want a comfortable rest instead of a late-night drive back to Bangkok? Check out well-located stays in Chai Nat town and along the Chao Phraya in advance — prices are friendly, and booking ahead gets you the better rooms.

faq.q: What can't-miss places are there in Chai Nat?
faq.a: The must-visits are Chai Nat Bird Park at the foot of Khao Tha Phra in Mueang district — a 26-rai open aviary billed as the largest in Asia, gathering over 100 bird species, plus a water park, a bird-egg museum, and the Chao Phraya Basin fish aquarium — and Chao Phraya Dam on the Sapphaya side, Thailand's first river barrage, with a long walkway for catching the breeze and watching the sunset. These two are the province's icons that nearly everyone visiting Chai Nat stops at.

faq.q: What are Chai Nat's highlights besides the bird park?
faq.a: Beyond the bird park and Chao Phraya Dam, Chai Nat has plenty for temple and history lovers: Wat Pak Khlong Makham Thao of Luang Pu Suk Kesaro, whose ordination hall holds murals painted by Krom Luang Chumphon Khet Udomsak; Wat Thammamun Worawihan on the hillside by the Chao Phraya, with its 565-step stairway and Luang Pho Thammachak; Sankhaburi old town, home to Wat Phra Kaeo's square chedi in U Thong–Lopburi style and Wat Mahathat's star-fruit-ribbed prangs; plus the Sapphaya Old Police Station Market, open only the first Saturday–Sunday of the month, and Wat Phra Borommathat Worawihan, the guardian stupa of Chai Nat.

faq.q: Do Chai Nat attractions charge admission?
faq.a: Nearly every temple and historic site on this list is free, with donations as you wish — including Wat Thammamun, Wat Pak Khlong Makham Thao, Wat Phra Kaeo Sankhaburi, and Wat Mahathat Sankhaburi. Chao Phraya Dam and Bueng Krachap Yai are free as well. The ticketed stops are Chai Nat Bird Park — Thais ฿60, foreigners ฿150, water park paid separately — and the Chai Nat Muni National Museum, Thais ฿10, foreigners ฿80. The Sapphaya Old Police Station Market is free to enter, with snacks starting around ฿20–60, and Wat Phra Borommathat Worawihan is likewise free, donations welcome.

faq.q: How do you get to Chai Nat, and what's parking like?
faq.a: The most convenient way is driving your own or a rental car from Bangkok, taking about two and a half hours, because the sights are spread across several districts — Mueang Chai Nat, Sapphaya, Wat Sing, Sankhaburi, and Hankha. Most attractions, such as Chai Nat Bird Park, Chao Phraya Dam, and the various temples, have spacious free parking on site. Without a car, vans and coaches run from Bangkok to Chai Nat town, where you can continue by hired car or motorbike taxi to each spot — but it's less convenient than driving, since public transport within the province is limited.

faq.q: What time do Chai Nat attractions open?
faq.a: The temples generally open for worship from morning until evening every day. Chai Nat Bird Park opens roughly 08:00–18:00 — best in the morning when the air is cool and the birds are active. The Sapphaya Old Police Station Market (Green Dee Market) opens only the first Saturday–Sunday of the month, 15:00–20:00, so check the dates before going. Chao Phraya Dam is best in the evening for the sunset, or at dawn for cycling on the crest. Wat Phra Borommathat Worawihan opens daily around 06:30–18:00. It's wise to check each place's hours before setting out.
